This interesting phylogenetic analysis of a mumps outbreak in Washington will be of interest to a wide audience, especially those working at the intersection of pathogen genomics and public health. An array of classic and novel phylogenetic approaches supports the conclusions that mumps was introduced several times in Washington during the outbreak, and that the Washington Marshallese community was particularly at risk of mumps infection and transmission despite high vaccination coverage. Consultation with a community health advocate from the affected communities helps contextualize the results.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Repeated introductions and intensive community transmission fueled a mumps virus outbreak in Washington State" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Miles Davenport as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1. Please rephrase conclusions regarding the role of age and vaccination to indicate the effect is inconclusive given the low power of the study/small sample size.

2. Figure 2 is difficult to read. A different color scheme may make this figure more understandable.

3. Please compare the age distribution of sampled cases vs outbreak cases in either supplementary table 2 or 3, this would help better convince readers that the sample is representative of the outbreak cases.

4. Elaborate on the decision to include tips on an internal node as the measured variable as opposed to tips with a branch length of a certain distance.

5. Rephrase heading on line 338

6. Additional contextualization of the problem of sampling bias and how this approach is different may help strengthen the methodology presented in the paper.

7. There were several other mumps outbreaks in the United States in the same 2016-2017 time period. Some discussion about Washington state particularities that prevented mumps transmission outside of the Marshallese community would be warranted.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

I cannot comment much on the sequencing and phylogenetic analyses as this is not my area of expertise, but I can comment on the epidemiological analyses:

• There is an overreliance on p-values in the interpretation of the logistic regression in Table 1. There is no consideration of the fact that the study does not have an adequate sample size to assess the effects of variables other than community status. I would recommend the authors do a post-hoc sample size power calculation, not necessarily to put in the article, but to convince themselves of whether they have the statistical power to assess the impact of vaccination and age. Basically, their logistic regression model is suggesting that in fact we cannot exclude the possibility that vaccination status and age may potentially have very strong effects on transmission (point estimate ORs of 2.21, 0.46, or 0.30, in other words over a doubling or a halving of the odds, which would be considered by many to be an important effect size). The only reason that the analysis has enough statistical power for community status is because the odds ratio is enormous and the prevalence of Marshallese samples is very high. Please read Amrhein V, Greenland S, McShane B. Nature. 2019 Mar;567(7748):305-307 for further discussion on this topic. I would suggest addressing this issue by:

– Mentioning low statistical power to assess the effects of age and vaccination as a limitation of this analysis

– When discussing the results for age and vaccination status, I would recommend using the suggestion of Amrhein et al. and to discuss the point estimate and confidence intervals rather than commenting on their non-statistical significance. (e.g. instead of "Neither age nor vaccination status were significantly associated with the presence of downstream tips in the tree", say instead that while those with unknown vaccination status were more likely to have descendants in the tree than those with known up-to-date vaccination, the confidence interval could not exclude a null or positive association between vaccination status and having tree descendants).

– The conclusion the authors should reach in the abstract and discussion is not that "Neither vaccination status nor age were strong determinants of transmission", but rather that while age and vaccination status might be associated with transmission, the authors did not have enough statistical power to estimate their effect (i.e. the confidence intervals are very wide and cannot exclude either no association or inverse associations).

• I find the parameterization of age very unusual, in general what is more often used for continuous variables is centering the variable around the mean or mode rather than normalizing. I am not convinced that age as a continuous variable is the best way to parameterize age for this analysis. There is no reason to believe that age would necessarily have a linear effect on transmission. Social networks and contacts do not change linearly with age but probably in a more segmented manner as individuals age into different life stages (school, workforce, retirement). Waning vaccine immunity is also possibly not linear with age. This is just a suggestion, but I think it would potentially be more fruitful and maybe yield higher statistical power in this case to categorize age dichotomously as either children (<20y) or adults (>=20y) based on different social networks in children vs adults. However, there may be other cutpoints that fit the data better and that could be explored. Otherwise, some justification for the parameterization of age would be nice.

• Please compare the age distribution of sampled cases vs outbreak cases in either supplementary table 2 or 3, this would help better convince readers that the sample is representative of the outbreak cases.

• Figure 2: Please make the data for Washington state more obvious, for example by restricting an entire color shade such as blue. Currently it is very difficult to distinguish between Georgia, Virginia, Manitoba, Washington, Massachusetts, and North Dakota. It is also not clear from the legend what a grey node represents.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The input from community health advocates is a strength that could be better highlighted in the discussion. It is unclear which potential causes (possibly all of them) are corroborated by the lived experiences of the individuals in the Marshallese community in WA.

The new test for descendants in the divergence tree is a useful method that is likely to be adopted in other studies. It would be nice if the authors could elaborate very briefly on the decision to include tips on an internal node as the measured variable as opposed to tips with a branch length of a certain distance. Is this decision based on the substitution rate and serial interval of Mumps and if applied by others should it be adjusted based on the pathogen and/or sampling scheme (e.g. Intensely sampling a super spreading event would show a large number of tips of one type at the base of 1 transmission chain which is different than finding many tips with descendants spread throughout the tree)?

The wording in the heading on line 338 is confusing.

Is it known, or suspected from interviews, if members of the Marshallese community are more closely connected through social contacts with each other than they are with the wider public? This seems like an implicit assumption, but very likely given the outbreaks in WA and AR.

Lines 667-668 in the methods mention 27 "states" were used in the phylogeographic reconstruction. The main text and Figure 1 mention 26.

results.result: The 2016/2017 Washington State mumps outbreak involved 889 confirmed and probable cases, with highest incidence among children aged 10-19 years despite high vaccination rates (91% up-to-date among cases aged 5-19). Marshallese individuals comprised 52% of cases despite representing only 0.3% of the state population, with 93% of Marshallese cases aged 5-19 being up-to-date on vaccination.
results.evaluation: The epidemiological characterization is well-supported by surveillance data presented throughout the manuscript. The claims about case counts, age distribution, vaccination rates, and disproportionate impact on the Marshallese community are consistently documented with specific percentages and incidence rates. The data sources are clearly identified as coming from Washington State Department of Health surveillance systems.

results.result: The study sequenced 166 mumps virus genomes: 110 from Washington State and 56 from other US states collected between 2006 and 2018.
results.evaluation: This is directly stated in multiple sections of the manuscript and represents the core dataset for the genomic analyses. The methods section provides detailed protocols for sample selection, sequencing, and quality control, with sequences deposited in public databases.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis revealed approximately 13 independent introductions of mumps into Washington State (95% HPD: 12-15), primarily from Arkansas. Four Arkansas introductions accounted for 92/110 sequenced cases and led to sustained transmission chains, while non-Arkansas introductions resulted exclusively in non-Marshallese infections with limited onward transmission. The primary outbreak clade was introduced from Arkansas around August 2016, approximately 3.5 months before the first reported case.
results.evaluation: The phylogeographic reconstruction using discrete trait models in BEAST is methodologically sound and the results are clearly presented with appropriate uncertainty estimates (HPD intervals). The finding of multiple introductions is supported by phylogenetic evidence shown in Figure 3, and the temporal estimates are consistent with molecular clock analyses. The differential success of Arkansas vs. non-Arkansas introductions is supported by the phylogenetic data.

results.result: Most Washington sequences nested within North American genotype G diversity circulating since 2006, but nine Washington sequences were highly divergent (TMRCA ~22 years), with seven clustering with New Zealand viruses suggesting travel-related introductions. Three non-genotype G viruses were also detected (genotypes A, H, and K).
results.evaluation: The phylogenetic placement of sequences is well-supported by maximum likelihood and time-resolved phylogenies shown in Figures 2 and supplementary figures. The identification of divergent sequences and their relationship to global diversity is appropriately documented. The inference of travel-related introductions for New Zealand-related sequences is reasonable but appropriately presented as speculative.

results.result: SH gene sequences showed insufficient resolution for fine-grained geographic inference, with almost all North American SH genes being identical and forming a single polytomy. The authors recommend that full-genome sequencing would be more useful than CDC-recommended SH-based genotyping for resolving local transmission patterns.
results.evaluation: The comparison between full-genome and SH-only phylogenies (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) clearly demonstrates the lack of resolution in SH sequences. This finding is consistent with previous studies cited by the authors. The recommendation for full-genome sequencing is a reasonable inference from the data, though it represents a suggestion for future practice rather than a tested result.

results.result: Using a novel 'basal tip' metric, Marshallese cases were significantly more likely to be upstream in transmission chains than non-Marshallese cases (odds ratio = 3.2, p=0.00725). While 56% of Marshallese tips were ancestral to downstream samples, only 27% of non-Marshallese tips were ancestral. Community membership was a significant determinant of sustained transmission when controlling for vaccination status and age.
results.evaluation: The development and application of the basal/terminal tip metric is methodologically sound and well-justified in the methods section. The logistic regression analysis appropriately controls for potential confounders (vaccination status and age) and reports effect sizes with confidence intervals. The statistical significance is properly assessed with p-values. However, the authors acknowledge that the dataset may be underpowered to fully resolve effects of vaccination and age.

results.result: Structured coalescent analysis showed that 84% (74/88) of internal nodes were inferred to circulate within the Marshallese community with high posterior probability (≥0.95). Transmission was predominantly unidirectional, with 29 estimated transmission events from Marshallese to non-Marshallese groups (95% HPD: 21-37) versus only 6 in the opposite direction (95% HPD: 0-14). The effective population size for non-Marshallese was approximately three times higher than for Marshallese, suggesting higher transmission rates within the Marshallese community.
results.evaluation: The structured coalescent analyses using BEAST are methodologically rigorous, with appropriate model specifications and multiple independent runs to assess convergence. The results are robust to different migration rate priors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and to subsampling to equalize Marshallese and non-Marshallese tips (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). The interpretation of effective population size differences is appropriately cited to Volz 2012 and the directional transmission pattern is strongly supported by the data.

results.result: Individuals with different vaccination statuses did not cluster together phylogenetically, suggesting no genetic difference between viruses infecting vaccinated versus unvaccinated individuals.
results.evaluation: The phylogenetic distribution of cases by vaccination status (Figure 7) clearly shows dispersion throughout the tree rather than clustering. This observation is straightforward and well-supported by the visual evidence. The inference that there is no genetic difference between viruses in different vaccination groups is reasonable, though the small number of not-up-to-date individuals limits statistical power.

results.result: The study concludes that contact networks and social networks are critical determinants of mumps transmission, and can be the primary risk factor for respiratory virus outbreaks even when vaccines are effective and widely used.
results.evaluation: This conclusion is well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple analyses showing sustained transmission within the Marshallese community despite high vaccination rates. The phylogenetic, epidemiological, and structured coalescent analyses all point to the importance of contact structure. However, this represents an inference from the data rather than direct measurement of contact networks.

results.result: The authors conclude that contact structures and historic disparities may leave populations at increased risk for respiratory virus disease even with effective, widely-used vaccines. They speculate that while waning immunity may promote outbreaks in young adults, outbreaks in younger age groups may be possible in high-contact settings.
results.evaluation: While the data clearly show high vaccination rates among cases and disproportionate impact on the Marshallese community, the specific role of waning immunity versus contact structure cannot be definitively separated with the available data. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation, stating they were unable to evaluate the precise effects of age and vaccination status. The speculation about younger age groups in high-contact settings is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive historical and social context about the Marshallese community, including US nuclear testing (1947-1986), health disparities, exclusion from Medicaid (1996-2020), larger household sizes (average 5.28 vs 2.52 for US), close-knit community structure, poor healthcare access, and hesitancy to seek care. These factors are proposed as potential contributors to increased mumps transmission intensity.
results.evaluation: The historical and demographic information is well-documented with appropriate citations to published literature and government sources. The authors appropriately consulted with Marshallese community health advocates to contextualize their findings. However, the specific contribution of each factor to mumps transmission is speculative and not directly measured. The authors appropriately present these as potential explanations rather than proven mechanisms.

results.result: The authors recommend that outbreak dose vaccination for high-risk groups may be especially effective for limiting mumps transmission in future outbreaks, noting that others have reported success with this approach and that CDC currently recommends this strategy. They also note that federal legislation restoring Medicaid access for Marshallese individuals was passed in December 2020.
results.evaluation: The recommendation for outbreak dose vaccination is appropriately supported by citations to previous successful implementations and current CDC guidelines. However, this represents a policy recommendation based on the study's findings rather than a tested intervention. The information about Medicaid legislation is factual and properly cited.

results.result: Mumps genomes accumulate mutations at a rate of 3.75 × 10⁻⁴ substitutions per site per year.
results.evaluation: This evolutionary rate estimate is derived from root-to-tip regression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, which is a standard approach for molecular clock estimation. The rate is consistent with previous mumps studies and is used appropriately throughout the phylogenetic analyses.

results.result: The authors address potential sampling bias concerns, noting that Washington uses passive surveillance (which causes underreporting), that Marshallese individuals may be particularly underreported due to lower healthcare-seeking behavior, but that their sampling strategy and use of structured coalescent methods (which are robust to sampling differences) mitigate these concerns.
results.evaluation: The discussion of sampling bias is thorough and appropriately cites relevant literature. The authors employed multiple strategies to address bias: uniform sampling across groups, structured coalescent methods shown to be robust to sampling differences, and sensitivity analyses with equal sampling. However, if Marshallese cases were substantially underreported, this would make the observed patterns even stronger, as the authors note.

results.result: The authors conclude that most introductions sparked short transmission chains, suggesting mumps did not transmit efficiently among the general Washington population, possibly due to more diffuse contact patterns. They note that mumps historically causes outbreaks in communities with strong contact patterns and dense housing, and that most 2016 US outbreaks were in university settings.
results.evaluation: The observation that most introductions led to short chains is well-supported by the phylogenetic data in Figure 3. The comparison to historical outbreak patterns is appropriately cited. However, the explanation involving diffuse contact patterns is speculative and not directly measured. The authors appropriately present this as a hypothesis rather than a proven mechanism.

results.result: The authors note that SARS-CoV-2 continues to disproportionately impact populations in high-risk settings, including the Marshallese, and that vaccine distribution alone may not be sufficient.
results.evaluation: This claim is supported by citations to relevant COVID-19 studies (Center et al., 2020; McElfish et al., 2021). However, this represents contextual information about the broader implications of the findings rather than a result of the current study.
